title: Jumbo Jets and a Shrinking World
summary: In 1969 a giant plane called the jumbo jet took off, big enough to carry hundreds of people at once. Bigger planes and cheap airlines made tickets cheaper, so millions of families could fly on holiday or visit faraway relatives. Soon the whole world felt closer together.

sections.heading: A Plane Two and a Half Times Too Big
paragraphs: In the mid-1960s, the jet age was already here. The Boeing 707 and the Douglas DC-8 were carrying travellers across oceans at more than 900 km/h, and airports were getting busier every year. But there was a problem: there were so many passengers that airports were filling up with planes, and each 707 could carry only about 140 to 190 people. Juan Trippe, the bold head of Pan American World Airways (Pan Am), had a very big idea. He wanted a jet roughly two and a half times the size of the 707.

Why so big? Trippe's reasoning was simple. Flying a plane costs a lot of money no matter how many people are inside: you need pilots, fuel, maintenance and a slot at the airport. If you can squeeze many more seats into one plane without needing many more pilots or much more fuel per person, every single seat becomes cheaper to fly. Cheaper seats mean cheaper tickets, and cheaper tickets mean more people can afford to travel.

In April 1966, Pan Am ordered 25 of the new giants for about 525 million US dollars, an enormous sum at the time. Because Pan Am was the first customer, it had more say in the design than almost any airline before or since. Boeing handed the job to an engineer named Joe Sutter, who had been working on the smaller 737. Sutter and his team at first imagined a double-decker plane, but they soon chose a different shape: one very wide main deck, wide enough for two aisles and ten seats across in economy class. This was the birth of the wide-body airliner, a plane whose cabin is so wide that it needs two aisles instead of one.

There was one more surprise in the design. Many people at the time believed that supersonic airliners like Concorde would soon take over passenger flying, and that big subsonic jets would end up carrying mainly cargo. So Sutter's team planned ahead. They lifted the cockpit up above the main deck, which gave the 747 its famous hump. With the pilots sitting up high, the whole nose of the plane could swing upward like a giant door, letting freight be loaded straight in from the front. The supersonic future never really arrived for most travellers, but the hump became the 747's trademark, and the area behind the cockpit became a lounge or a cabin with extra seats.

Building the plane was a challenge as huge as the plane itself. No Boeing factory was big enough, so the company built a brand-new one near Paine Field in Everett, about 50 kilometres north of Seattle in Washington State. It is still the largest building in the world measured by volume. The thousands of workers who designed and built the first 747s in a hurry, in under three years, were nicknamed “the Incredibles.”

On 9 February 1969, test pilots Jack Waddell and Brien Wygle took the first 747 into the air over Washington. The plane was about 70 metres long, its wings stretched about 60 metres from tip to tip, and its tail stood about as tall as a six-storey building. Reporters quickly gave it a nickname that stuck forever: the jumbo jet.

sections.heading: Queen of the Skies
paragraphs: Imagine walking into Pan Am's first 747 in New York in January 1970. After years of narrow, tube-like cabins, the space would have seemed astonishing: two aisles, rows of seats stretching far ahead, and, if you were lucky enough to travel first class, a spiral staircase leading up to a lounge in the hump. The first passenger service, from New York to London, took off on 22 January 1970, about six hours late because of an overheating engine on the plane originally planned for the trip. Even a giant can have first-day jitters.

The secret behind the 747 was not just its size but its engines. It was designed around the Pratt and Whitney JT9D, one of the first big high-bypass turbofans. You met turbofans in Part 15: a large fan at the front pushes most of the air around the outside of the hot engine core instead of through it. Moving a large amount of air fairly slowly is much more efficient than moving a small amount of air very fast. Engineers expected these engines to give roughly twice the push of older jet engines while burning about a third less fuel. Four of them hung under the 747's wings.

How many people could it carry? That depended on how an airline arranged the seats. A typical three-class layout held about 366 passengers, and later versions with a stretched upper deck and tightly packed economy seats could carry well over 400. Some Japanese airlines flew special short-distance 747s on busy domestic routes with more than 500 seats.

There was a catch, and it nearly sank Boeing. A jumbo jet was only cheap to fly when it was full. Figures from the time showed that a 747 flying 70 percent full still burned over 95 percent of the fuel of a completely full one. Soon after the 747 entered service, a recession hit, fewer people travelled and airlines had trouble filling their giant new planes. Boeing had spent so much developing the 747 that it had to lay off tens of thousands of workers around Seattle. Around that time, a famous billboard near the city joked: “Will the last person leaving Seattle turn out the lights.”

But travel bounced back, and the 747 became one of the most successful airliners ever. Airlines learned to fill seats by lowering fares, offering package holidays and selling cheap tickets to people who could book early. The jumbo carried rock bands, presidents, pilgrims, students and grandparents. Cargo versions with the swing-up nose carried racehorses, car parts and even, on one modified 747, a NASA Space Shuttle riding piggyback on its back.

Boeing kept improving the design for more than half a century, from the 747-100 to the 747-400 with its upturned wingtips and, finally, the 747-8. The last one, a cargo plane for Atlas Air, was delivered on 31 January 2023, ending a 54-year production run. In total 1,574 were built. Pilots and fans still call it the Queen of the Skies.

sections.heading: Europe Joins the Race: Airbus
paragraphs: In the 1960s, American companies such as Boeing, Douglas and Lockheed built most of the world's airliners. European countries had brilliant engineers, but each country's aircraft industry was small on its own. Britain's de Havilland had built the first jet airliner, the Comet, and Britain and France were working together on Concorde, but no single European company could match the giant American factories.

So European governments decided to team up. On 18 December 1970, France and West Germany formed Airbus Industrie, each holding half. Spain's CASA joined in 1971, and Britain joined in 1979. Instead of one company building everything, each partner built different pieces. Wings might come from Britain, parts of the body from Germany, the tail from Spain, and final assembly happened in Toulouse in the south of France.

That raised a funny problem: how do you move a whole section of an airliner's body from Hamburg to Toulouse? Airbus answered with one of the strangest-looking aircraft ever flown, the Super Guppy. It was built from an old Boeing propeller airliner with a gigantic bulging body on top, a bit like a pregnant whale with wings. Its nose swung open so that huge plane parts could slide inside. Because parts arrived just when they were needed for assembly, the A300 is described as the first airliner built with a “just-in-time” system.

The first Airbus plane, the A300, first flew on 28 October 1972 and began carrying passengers with Air France between Paris and London on 23 May 1974. It was a wide-body jet with two aisles, like the 747, but with an important difference: it had only two engines instead of four. In fact, it was the world's first twin-engine wide-body airliner. Two big modern turbofans used less fuel and needed less maintenance than three or four engines, which made the A300 cheap to run on busy medium-distance routes.

At first sales were slow, and many airlines were unsure about buying a European plane. Then, in 1977, the American airline Eastern Air Lines borrowed four A300s to try them out, liked them and ordered more. That was a turning point. In the following decades Airbus added more models, including the A320 family of narrow-body jets in the 1980s, which became one of the best-selling airliner families ever.

By the 2000s, the airliner business had become a contest between two giants, Boeing in the United States and Airbus in Europe. Each company tries to build planes that use less fuel, carry the right number of people and fly the right distances for what airlines want. That competition has pushed both companies to make quieter, more efficient planes and has helped keep the price of new aircraft from rising even faster. In total, 561 A300s were delivered before production ended in 2007.

sections.heading: The Double-Decker Giant: the A380
paragraphs: If the 747 was a jumbo, what would be bigger? In the 1990s Airbus decided to beat Boeing at its own game. It designed the A380, the only full-length double-deck jet airliner ever built. From nose to tail, both levels of the plane are full passenger cabins, connected by staircases.

The A380 first flew on 27 April 2005 from Toulouse. Its wingspan, about 80 metres, was carefully kept just under a limit of 80 metres agreed for the largest airport gates, so it could still fit into big airports. Even so, many airports had to rebuild gates with two-level boarding bridges, strengthen taxiways and widen runway edges to handle it.

Singapore Airlines received the first A380 in October 2007 and flew the first passenger service, flight SQ380 from Singapore to Sydney, on 25 October 2007. A typical layout held about 525 passengers in three classes, but the plane was certified to carry up to 853 people if every seat were packed in economy. Some airlines used the extra space for luxuries that seemed impossible in a plane: showers for first-class passengers, private suites with doors, and bars where travellers could stand and chat high above the ocean.

Yet the A380 never sold as well as Airbus had hoped. Only 254 were built, and the last one was delivered to Emirates, its biggest customer, on 16 December 2021. Why did such an amazing plane struggle?

Part of the answer is a big debate about how people will fly. Airbus bet that travellers would keep flying through a few giant hub airports, such as London Heathrow, Dubai or Singapore, where enormous planes would carry crowds between the hubs. Boeing bet that people would rather fly directly between more cities without changing planes, using medium-sized, very efficient twin-engine jets like the Boeing 777 and 787. Over time, Boeing's prediction turned out to be closer to what most airlines wanted.

Modern twin-engine jets also changed the rules. Engines became so reliable that safety regulators allowed two-engine planes to fly routes far from any airport, even across oceans, which once had been flown mainly by three- and four-engine jets. A twin-engine plane with 300 seats is easier to fill than a giant with 500, and it burns less fuel overall. When the A380's biggest customers stopped ordering more, Airbus announced in 2019 that it would end production.

The A380 did not fail at flying. Passengers love its quiet, roomy cabin, and many are still in service. But its story teaches an important lesson about inventions: a machine has to fit the way people actually want to live and travel, not just be the biggest or most impressive.

sections.heading: Flying for Everyone: the Low-Cost Airlines
paragraphs: For much of the 20th century, a plane ticket was something many families saved up for over many months. In many countries, governments controlled which airlines could fly which routes and even what prices they could charge. Airlines competed with fancy meals and friendly service rather than low fares.

A few rebels showed that things could be different. Pacific Southwest Airlines, which started flying inside California on 6 May 1949, is often called the world's first low-cost airline. Because it flew only within one state, it was not bound by the national fare rules. Its success inspired Herb Kelleher and Rollin King in Texas, who founded what became Southwest Airlines. Southwest started flying on 18 June 1971 between Dallas, Houston and San Antonio, again staying inside one state so it could set its own low prices.

In 1978 the United States passed the Airline Deregulation Act, which let airlines choose their own routes and fares. New airlines appeared, older ones had to compete, and prices for many trips fell. Across the Atlantic, the British businessman Freddie Laker launched his no-frills Skytrain between London and New York in 1977. It was eventually forced out of business, but it proved that cheap long-distance tickets could attract huge crowds. Europe opened up its own skies step by step in the late 1980s and 1990s, until any airline from one European Union country could fly between cities in other member countries.

That opened the door for Europe's budget airlines. EasyJet began in 1995, flying two Boeing 737s from Luton, near London, to Glasgow and Edinburgh, with the slogan that flying should be as affordable as a pair of jeans. Ryanair, an Irish airline founded in the 1980s, remade itself on the Southwest model and grew into Europe's largest budget airline by passenger numbers.

How can a low-cost airline sell such cheap tickets and still make money? It uses a whole box of tricks. Most budget airlines fly just one type of aircraft, so pilots, mechanics and spare parts can all be shared. They fly mostly short, direct routes and often use smaller, cheaper airports a little outside big cities. They turn each plane around very quickly at the gate, so it can fly more trips each day, because a plane sitting on the ground earns nothing. They sell tickets online instead of paying travel agents, and they charge extra for checked bags, choosing a seat or snacks. Seats are packed a bit closer together. Every small saving adds up.

The result was a revolution. Students could visit friends in other countries for a weekend. Workers could go home to see their families more often. Cities that had never had many visitors suddenly filled with tourists. In 2017, airlines around the world carried about 4.1 billion passengers on roughly 42 million scheduled flights, and the number kept climbing to well over 4 billion in 2019. Flying, once a luxury for the rich, had become something ordinary people did every day.

sections.heading: A Shrinking World
paragraphs: Of course the Earth did not actually get smaller. But when a trip that once took weeks by ship takes only hours by plane, the world starts to feel smaller. In 1900, crossing the Atlantic by steamship took about a week. By the 1970s, a jumbo jet could do it in about seven or eight hours. A journey from London to Australia that once took more than a month by sea could be done in about a day.

This changed ordinary life in many ways. Holidays abroad, once rare, became normal for millions of families. Whole towns, like beach resorts in Spain or islands in the Caribbean and Southeast Asia, grew up around tourists arriving by air. At the same time, families began to spread out across the globe. A grandmother might live in India while her grandchildren grow up in Canada, and a flight lets them meet in person instead of only by letter or video call. Students travel to universities on other continents, scientists fly to meetings, and sports teams play matches on the other side of the world the same week.

Planes also carry things, not just people. A large share of air cargo, often around half, travels in the bellies of passenger planes, under the passengers' feet, and the rest in dedicated freighters like the cargo 747. In 1971 a young American named Frederick W. Smith founded Federal Express (now FedEx) based on a simple idea: one company should pick up a package, fly it on its own planes overnight through a central hub, and deliver it the next morning. FedEx started flying on 17 April 1973 with 14 small jets serving 25 American cities. On its first night it carried just 186 packages. Today overnight delivery of letters, parcels and online shopping is something people take for granted.

Air freight is especially useful for things that are valuable, urgent or that spoil quickly. Fresh roses grown in Kenya or Colombia can be in a shop in Europe or North America within a couple of days of being cut. Fresh fish, strawberries out of season, newspapers, mobile phones, medicines, vaccines and even human organs for transplant operations travel by air. Factories around the world depend on parts delivered just in time, sometimes by plane.

There were deeper changes too. When people can travel easily, ideas, music, food and languages travel with them. Business meetings, scientific conferences and international friendships all became easier. Some historians say that cheap flights helped turn the world into one connected global economy. Of course, as later parts will show, flying also brings new problems. But there is no doubt that the jet age changed where people live, how they work and whom they meet.

sections.heading: The Hidden Machinery of Flying
paragraphs: A modern flight is the tip of an iceberg. Underneath every trip lies a huge system of other inventions, rules and workers that grew up because of airplanes.

Start with the airport. As more cities got flights, airlines realised they could not fly directly between every pair of cities. Delta was one of the first to build a hub-and-spoke system, using Atlanta as its hub. Picture a bicycle wheel: the hub is the middle, and the spokes reach out to the rim. Planes fly from many small spoke cities into the hub, passengers change planes there, and then fly out to their final destinations. This lets an airline connect hundreds of cities with far fewer routes and planes. It is why some airports, such as Atlanta, Dubai and Istanbul, have become enormous transfer stations where most passengers never even leave the terminal. In 2025, Atlanta alone handled about 106 million passengers, counting both arrivals and departures.

Next, how do you get onto the plane without walking across a windy, rainy apron? The answer is the jet bridge, a moving, enclosed corridor that stretches from the terminal right to the plane's door. An engineer named Frank Der Yuen is credited with inventing it. United Airlines tested a prototype in 1954, and the first working one opened at Chicago's O'Hare Airport in 1958. Its end can swing, rise, fall and stretch so it can fit planes of many different sizes, from small jets to the double-deck A380.

Then there is booking a seat. In the early days of airlines, reservations were tracked on paper cards in giant rotating files, and making a booking could take about 90 minutes. In 1953, an IBM salesman named Blair Smith happened to sit next to C. R. Smith, the president of American Airlines, on a flight from Los Angeles to New York. The two men (not related) talked about using computers to keep track of every passenger's reservation. The result was SABRE, which went online experimentally in 1960 and became fully working in 1964. It was the world's first fully working computer reservation system. Bookings that had taken an hour and a half now took seconds. Systems like it were among the first giant business computer networks, years before the internet.

Finally, airplanes cross borders, so countries had to agree on rules. Even before World War II ended, 52 countries signed the Convention on International Civil Aviation, often called the Chicago Convention, on 7 December 1944 in Chicago. It created the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which began work on 4 April 1947 and became part of the United Nations system. ICAO sets common standards that almost every country follows, such as pilot licensing, rules of the air, airport design, aircraft registration and accident investigation. Thanks to agreements like these, a pilot from Brazil and a controller in Japan can understand each other, usually in English, which became the common language of international aviation.

Almost nobody thinks about these hidden inventions while waiting for a flight. Yet without hubs, jet bridges, booking computers and shared rules, the jumbo jet could never have carried billions of people.

sections.heading: When the Sky Went Quiet
paragraphs: Being so well connected has a downside. Anything people carry with them can travel quickly too, including germs. In the Middle Ages, a disease might take months or years to cross a continent along trade routes. In the jet age, a traveller can catch an illness in one country and be on the other side of the world before even feeling sick.

This became very clear in early 2020. A new coronavirus, which causes the illness COVID-19, was first identified in the city of Wuhan, China, at the end of 2019. Within weeks, cases appeared in many countries, partly because infected travellers carried the virus on planes before anyone knew how widely it had spread. On 11 March 2020 the World Health Organization declared a pandemic, which means a disease spreading across the whole world.

To slow the virus, countries closed their borders and told people to stay home. Canada closed its border to most foreign travellers on 16 March 2020, and Australia closed its borders to non-residents on 20 March. Within weeks, flying almost stopped. In April 2020, the number of seats offered by airlines around the world was down by about 91 percent compared to normal. Airports that usually roared with activity fell eerily silent. Many families who were living apart suddenly could not visit each other at all.

With nowhere to fly, airlines had to park their planes. By mid-April 2020, roughly two out of every three mainline airliners in the world were sitting on the ground; at the peak, about 16,500 airliners were parked in storage. Rows of jumbo jets and A380s were lined up at airports and in desert storage yards in places like Arizona and Australia, where the dry air helps stop metal from rusting. Some older planes, including many 747s, never flew passengers again.

Over the whole year of 2020, the number of air passengers fell by more than half (about 60 percent by some counts). Airlines lost huge amounts of money, and many workers lost their jobs. Cargo flights, on the other hand, became even more important, carrying masks, medical supplies and later vaccines. Some airlines even took the seats out of passenger planes to fill the cabins with boxes.

Travel slowly came back as vaccines arrived and borders reopened. By 2023 and 2024, flying in many parts of the world had returned to roughly the levels of 2019. The pandemic showed two things at once: how deeply the world now depends on airplanes, and how they can carry dangers as well as people.

And that leads to some big questions. With tens of thousands of flights in the air every day, how do planes avoid bumping into each other? What happens when something goes wrong? And what are all those flights doing to the air we breathe and to the planet's climate? Part 18 takes a close look at safety, problems and the hard questions that come with the gift of flight.

deepDive: Why did bigger planes make flying cheaper? Airline economists measure cost per available seat-kilometre: the cost of moving one seat one kilometre. Many costs, such as the two or three pilots in the cockpit, landing fees and a large share of maintenance, are paid per flight, not per seat. Spread them across 400 seats instead of 150 and each seat gets cheaper. High-bypass turbofans added a second saving, because pushing a large mass of air slowly is more efficient than pushing a small mass fast, which is why the 747 was built around the JT9D. But the savings only appear when seats are filled. The load factor, the share of seats actually sold, matters enormously: a 747 that was 70 percent full still burned more than 95 percent of the fuel of a full one. That is why airlines invented discount fares, advance-purchase tickets and package tours, and why computer reservation systems that could juggle millions of bookings and prices became so valuable. Historians and economists still debate the best shape for an airline network. Hub-and-spoke systems connect many cities with few routes and help fill big planes, but they force passengers to change planes and concentrate delays at a few airports. Point-to-point networks are more convenient for travellers but need many medium-sized, efficient aircraft. Airbus's A380 was a bet on hubs; Boeing's 787 was a bet on point-to-point. The fact that 1,574 747s were built over 54 years but only 254 A380s suggests the market moved toward medium-sized twin-engine jets, helped by rules that let very reliable twins fly far from airports over oceans. Counting passengers is also trickier than it looks. Airline statistics count each person once per flight, giving roughly 4 to 4.5 billion passenger trips around 2019, while airport statistics count each traveller twice, once leaving and once arriving, which is why airport groups reported about 9.1 billion airport passengers in 2019. Neither number means 4 or 9 billion different people: many travellers fly dozens of times a year, while most people on Earth have still never flown.
funFact: The factory Boeing built in Everett, Washington, to make the 747 is the largest building in the world measured by volume.
